title: Scope and hoisting
summary: Where a variable lives and when it exists: block scope, var, hoisting and the temporal dead zone.

concepts.title: Block scope with let and const

misconceptions.description: Believes a let or const declared inside braces is still visible after the closing brace.
Believes var stays inside the braces of an if or loop, like let.
Believes a var declared inside a function becomes a global variable.
Believes a var keeps its value from one call of a function to the next.
Believes a variable declared inside a block with the same name replaces the outer variable.
Believes a redeclared name inside a block is ignored and the outer variable is used.
Believes a variable that is out of scope still exists and reads as undefined.
Reads the value a variable had before the traced line ran instead of after it.
Believes a declaration does not exist until the line that writes it has run.
Believes hoisting moves the assigned value of a var, not only its name.
Believes a function stored in a const can be called before its line, like a function declaration.
Believes reading a let or const before its line gives undefined, like var.
Believes code written above a let declaration can never read it, even if it runs later.
Believes a let variable keeps its first value after it is assigned a new one.

lessons.title: Block scope with let and const

conceptCard.title: let and const stay in their braces
conceptCard.body: A variable declared with let or const exists only inside the braces where it is written. Code outside the block cannot see it. A block may reuse a name from outside; inside, the new variable hides the outer one.

conceptCard.title: var belongs to the whole function
conceptCard.body: var ignores braces. A var declared inside an if or a loop is visible in the whole function around it, and nowhere outside. Older code uses var a lot, so you need to read it, even if let is the better choice.

conceptCard.title: Declarations are set up first
conceptCard.body: Before a scope runs, JavaScript sets up its declarations. A function declaration is ready to call from the first line. A var exists too, but holds undefined until its own line runs.

conceptCard.title: Touching let too early throws
conceptCard.body: let and const are set up early as well, but cannot be used until their declaration line has run. The gap is the temporal dead zone, and reading in it throws a ReferenceError. It depends on when code runs, not where it is written.

options.text: peek can read cap because it runs after line 2 has run.
options.feedback: Right. What counts is when the code runs, not where it is written.

options.text: Code written above a let declaration can never read it.
options.feedback: You thought a read written above a let line can never work. What matters is whether the let line has run by the time the read runs.

options.text: peek gives NaN, because let is hoisted without a value.
options.feedback: You thought a let is hoisted with an undefined value, as a var is. A let has no such state: a read before its line is an error, and a read after it sees the value.

items.prompt: What does total hold right after line 6 has run?

options.feedback: Right. The dead zone of price ends when line 5 runs. bill reads price only when line 6 calls it, after line 5 has stored 4, so it returns 8.
This treats the dead zone as a matter of where code is written: bill sits above the let line. The dead zone is about when a read runs, compared with when the let line has run.
This reads price as undefined, the way a var reads before its line. A let has no undefined phase: before its line runs, any read of it throws.

items.explanation: The dead zone of price lasts from the start of its scope until line 5 runs. bill reads price only when line 6 calls it, after line 5 has stored 4, so the read is allowed and bill returns 8. What counts is when the read runs, not where the function is written.
hints: Look at line 6 and ask which lines have already run when bill reads price.
A let binding cannot be read until its own line has run; time decides, not position in the file.
Compare the moment line 5 runs with the moment the return on line 2 runs.
